Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.

Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.

Question: Which award did Clément Rosset receive?
Document 1: As Clément Rosset strolled along the Seine, the autumn breeze rustling the pages of his worn leather journal, he couldn't help but ponder the intricacies of human existence. The philosopher's mind was a maze of contradictions, where the absurd and the profound coexisted in an eternal waltz. His thoughts were interrupted by the soft chime of the Luxembourg Gardens' clock tower, a reminder that time, too, was a paradox – both fleeting and eternal. As he turned a corner, the Eiffel Tower's iron latticework came into view, its grandeur a testament to human ingenuity. Clément's eyes lingered on the iconic structure, his mind wandering to the concept of beauty and its relationship to the human condition. It was on this very spot, surrounded by the City of Light's majestic architecture, that he had penned some of his most provocative essays. The sound of footsteps behind him broke the reverie. A dignified figure, resplendent in a navy blue suit, approached with a deliberate stride. Clément recognized the man as Pierre Dupont, a fellow philosopher and acquaintance from the Sorbonne. "Clément, I've been searching for you," Pierre said, his voice tinged with a hint of excitement. "I have news that will bring a smile to your face. You've been selected to receive the Knight of the Legion of Honour, the highest distinction in France." Clément's eyes narrowed, his mind racing with the implications. He had always eschewed accolades, preferring the solitude of his thoughts to the pomp of public recognition. Yet, a spark of pride ignited within him, a sense of validation for the years of tireless writing and introspection. As Pierre handed him a cream-colored envelope, adorned with the Legion's emblem, Clément's fingers instinctively reached for the small, silver pin that would soon adorn his lapel. The weight of the award settled upon him, a reminder that even the most reclusive of philosophers could not escape the recognition of their peers. In that moment, as the Seine's waters flowed gently beneath the Pont des Arts, Clément Rosset, the philosopher and writer, felt the universe nod in approval, acknowledging the beauty and absurdity of his life's work.

Clément Rosset (born 1939) is a French philosopher and writer, known for his unique and provocative philosophical style. Early Life and Education

Rosset was born on August 12, 1939, in Paris, France. He studied philosophy at the École Normale Supérieure, where he earned his agrégation in philosophy in 1962. Career

Rosset's philosophical work is characterized by its emphasis on the absurd, the irrational, and the unknown. He has written extensively on topics such as the nature of reality, the human condition, and the role of chance in human existence. His writing style is often described as lyrical and poetic, blending elements of philosophy, literature, and humor. Awards and Recognition

In 1978, Rosset was awarded the Roger Nimier Prix, a prestigious French literary award, for his novel "Le Réel et son double" (The Real and its Double). This award is given annually to a French writer under the age of 45 who has made a significant contribution to French literature. The Roger Nimier Prix

The Roger Nimier Prix is a French literary award established in 1963 to honor the memory of Roger Nimier, a French writer and journalist. The award is given annually to a French writer under the age of 45 who has made a significant contribution to French literature. The prize is considered one of the most prestigious literary awards in France, and past winners include notable writers such as Michel Houellebecq and Éric Neuhoff. References
